content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a document in Geneva in 2009 addressing procurement and supply management for tuberculosis and malaria. This document was accessed in February 2012. 2. The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) released the 17th edition of the UN Recommendations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods: Model Regulations in 2011. This document was accessed in February 2012. 3. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations issued guidelines on good labeling practices for pesticides in 1995. These guidelines were accessed in February 2012. 4. The Collaborative International Pesticides Analytical Council (CIPAC) provides a handbook and guidelines for pesticide analysis. This resource was accessed in February 2012. 5. CIPAC, in collaboration with FAO and WHO, developed guidelines for the quality control of pesticide products, specifically for national laboratories. This document was accessed in February 2012. 6. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act Inspection Manual in Washington, DC, in 2002. This manual was accessed in February 2012. 7. The International Standards Organization (ISO) released a document in 2009 on random sampling and randomization procedures, identified as ISO 24153. 8. WHO conducted a technical consultation in 2005 on the specifications and quality control of netting materials and mosquito nets. This document was accessed in February 2012. 9. ISO published a document in 2006 titled Sampling Procedures for Inspection by Attributes – Part 10: Introduction to the ISO 2859 Series of Standards for Sampling for Inspection by Attributes, identified as ISO 2859-10. 10. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) released the 8th edition of the Infectious Substances Shipping Guidelines in 2007. 11. FAO's Desert Locust Control Committee held its 39th session in Rome in 2009. The related document was accessed in February 2012. 12. Guidelines for procuring public health pesticides include detailed annexes, such as documentation for inviting tenders for pesticide supply, price and delivery schedules, sampling reports, and chain-of-custody records. 13. Tender documentation must include a clear description of the product(s), the name and address of the organization inviting tenders, the reference number, and the supply period. Tenders must be submitted in sealed envelopes and delivered to the specified location by the deadline. 14. General conditions for tenders include the requirement for complete documentation, adherence to specifications, and submission of sufficient supporting evidence. Prices must include costs for packaging, labeling, insurance, transport, and delivery. 15. Contracts may not necessarily be awarded to the lowest bidder but will consider factors such as quality, effectiveness, safety, and compliance with specifications. 16. Tenders must remain valid for the specified period after the opening date. Shorter validity periods will result in rejection. 17. Tenderers bear all costs associated with preparing and submitting their tenders, regardless of the outcome. 18. Representatives of tenderers may witness the opening of tenders, and details such as tender prices and security presence will be announced. 19. Any attempt to influence the procurement entity during the evaluation process may result in rejection of the tender. 20. The procurement entity reserves the right to accept or reject any tender, annul the process, or reject all tenders before awarding the contract. 21. Contracts will not be awarded to tenderers found to have engaged in corrupt or fraudulent practices. 22. Successful tenderers must not use the award for advertising purposes. 23. Disputes arising from the tendering process will be resolved in the designated court. 24. The procurement entity reserves the right to examine, sample, and analyze products being procured. Suppliers must facilitate this process. 25. Non-compliant products must be removed and replaced by the supplier at their expense. If the supplier cannot meet specifications, they must refund the procurement entity for incurred expenses. 26. Suppliers must warrant that their products do not infringe on patents, designs, trade names, or trademarks. They must indemnify the procurement entity against any related claims. 27. Suppliers cannot assign or transfer the contract without written consent from the procurement entity. 28. If a supplier becomes insolvent, the procurement entity may terminate the contract immediately. 29. Sampling reports, chain-of-custody records, and analysis requests must follow specified formats to ensure proper documentation and traceability. 30. For detecting non-compliance in products such as mosquito nets, statistical sampling methods are used to achieve a specified confidence level. For example, testing 22 nets per batch provides 90% confidence in detecting 10% non-compliance.
